hints: Focus on the first test with water, a gas is evolved and the solution becomes alkaline, so think about what type of substance gives both products.
Remember that a metal reacting with water gives a hydroxide plus hydrogen, while a metal oxide reacting with water gives only a hydroxide with no gas.
Now use the second test with sulfuric acid, only one of the resulting hydroxides forms an insoluble white sulfate precipitate, recall the solubility of Group 2 sulfates.
walkthrough:
**Decode the reaction with water**

The pH increase tells us an alkali, a soluble hydroxide, has formed. The gas evolved must be hydrogen. That combination points to a reactive metal, not an oxide.

$$\text{M} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{M(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2$$

**Rule out the oxides**

Both barium oxide and magnesium oxide will dissolve or react to give hydroxides and raise pH, but no gas is produced.

$$\text{MO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{M(OH)}_2$$
So options B and D cannot fit the gas observation.

**Use the sulfate precipitate test**

The alkaline solution is $\text{M(OH)}_2$. Adding $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ tests for an insoluble Group 2 sulfate. Barium gives insoluble white barium sulfate, magnesium gives soluble magnesium sulfate.

$$\text{Ba(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Confirm the reactivity match**

Barium is a very reactive Group 2 metal and reacts readily with cold water to give $\text{H}_2$ gas. Magnesium reacts only extremely slowly with cold water, so no noticeable gas is seen. Only barium fits both observations.

options.A: Barium reacts with water to give soluble barium hydroxide (pH increases) and hydrogen gas. The hydroxide then reacts with sulfuric acid to give insoluble white barium sulfate precipitate. Both observations are matched perfectly.
options.B: Barium oxide does give barium hydroxide and would give the white BaSO4 precipitate later, but its reaction with water produces no gas. This fails the first observation.
options.C: Magnesium is a metal so in theory it could give H2, but it reacts far too slowly with cold water to show this. Also, Mg(OH)2 with sulfuric acid gives soluble MgSO4, so no white precipitate forms.
options.D: Magnesium oxide reacts with water to give Mg(OH)2 with no gas evolved, and the product with sulfuric acid is soluble MgSO4. It fails on both the gas test and the precipitate test.
